evidence.effect: AI accuracy was 81.6% in males vs 63.0% in females (p<0.001). Accuracy was lower with increasing age (true 63.54 vs false 69.40 years, p<0.001). Accuracy was higher for left- than right-sided fractures (72.5% vs 65.6%, p=0.029).
evidence.quote: Age did not impact the radiologists’ diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.802); however, AI showed a decrease in accuracy with increasing patient age (p < 0.001) ( Fig 4 and Table 3 ).

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT 4.0 Diagnose Epilepsy? A Study on Artificial Intelligence's Diagnostic Capabilities
evidence.outcome: Factors associated with ChatGPT diagnostic errors, including patient age and medical conditions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT made diagnostic errors in 41.7% of cases, more frequent in older patients and those with specific medical conditions; correct classification associated with acute symptomatic seizures of unknown etiology.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT made diagnostic errors in 41.7% of the cases, with errors more frequent in older patients and those with specific medical conditions.

evidence.title: Large language models improve the identification of emergency department visits for symptomatic kidney stones
evidence.outcome: Fairness of LLM performance across race and gender subgroups
evidence.effect: GPT-4 showed no racial or gender disparities; GPT-3.5 failed to effectively model racial diversity.
evidence.quote: Bias assessment found that GPT-4 exhibited no racial or gender disparities, in contrast to GPT-3.5, which failed to effectively model racial diversity.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Outperform Traditional Natural Language Processing Methods in Extracting Patient-Reported Outcomes in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
evidence.outcome: Model performance differences by demographics or diagnosis
evidence.effect: No biases were detected based on demographics or diagnosis.
evidence.quote: No biases were detected based on demographics or diagnosis.
evidence.sample_unit: clinic notes (50 UCSF test set, 250 Stanford external validation)

evidence.title: Optimising test intervals for individuals with type 2 diabetes: A machine learning approach
evidence.outcome: Model fairness across income and education subgroups
evidence.effect: Fairness metric suggests models perform well in terms of equality across income and education levels; AUC ranged 0.53 to 0.89 across test intervals.
evidence.quote: The fairness metric suggests models perform well in terms of equality.

evidence.title: Emerging algorithmic bias: fairness drift as the next dimension of model maintenance and sustainability
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Subgroup performance gaps at initial validation by race and sex
evidence.effect: Specificity and accuracy higher for female vs male in all models; sensitivity lower for female in readmission and pneumonia models; no AUC, O:E, or ICI differences by race or sex.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity was lower for female vs male patients in models for readmission and pneumonia.

evidence.title: Large Language Models for Pediatric Differential Diagnoses in Rural Health Care: Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study Comparing GPT-3 With Pediatrician Performance
evidence.outcome: Model accuracy across age subgroups and common complaints
evidence.effect: Accuracy consistent across age groups: 0-5 years 54/62 (87%), 6-12 years 47/53 (89%), 13-18 years 30/35 (86%); fever 36/39 (92%), abdominal pain 20/23 (87%).
evidence.quote: Performance was consistent across age groups (0-5 years: 54/62, 87%; 6-12 years: 47/53, 89%; 13-18 years: 30/35, 86%) and common complaints (fever: 36/39, 92%; abdominal pain: 20/23, 87%).

evidence.title: Exploring Biases of Large Language Models in the Field of Mental Health: Comparative Questionnaire Study of the Effect of Gender and Sexual Orientation in Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa Case Vignettes
evidence.outcome: LLM output differences across gender and sexual orientation subgroups in vignettes
evidence.effect: Gender bias found in ChatGPT-4 RAND-36 mental composite (P=.04); none for sexual orientation (P=.71) or EDE-Q overall score; MentaLLaMA results unreliable.
evidence.quote: MentaLLaMA did not yield reliable results.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated questionnaire responses (ChatGPT-4 observations from 120 vignettes, each run thrice)

evidence.title: Analyzing clinical variables indicative of uveal melanoma to determine how they affect decisions made by an artificial intelligence classifier
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie
evidence.outcome: Association of lesion characteristics, demographics and risk factors with false-negative AI classifications
evidence.effect: 44 of 194 lesion eyes (23%) were false negatives. Thinner lesions were more often missed (p = 0.026). Imaging risk factors for uveal melanoma showed no significant association with false negatives.
evidence.quote: Thinner lesions were more likely to be missed by the model (p = 0.026), resulting in a FN classification.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with choroidal melanocytic lesions (388 fundus images total)

evidence.title: Sociodemographic biases in medical decision making by large language models
evidence.outcome: Differences in recommended imaging and testing by income label across LLMs
evidence.effect: High-income-labeled cases received significantly more advanced imaging (CT/MRI) recommendations (P < 0.001), while low- and middle-income-labeled cases were often limited to basic or no further testing.
evidence.quote: Similarly, cases labeled as having high-income status received significantly more recommendations (P < 0.001) for advanced imaging tests such as computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, while low- and middle-income-labeled cases were often limited to basic or no further testing.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department cases (each in 32 sociodemographic variations; >1.7 million model outputs)

evidence.title: Deep Learning-Based Glaucoma Detection Using Clinical Notes: A Comparative Study of Long Short-Term Memory and Convolutional Neural Network Models
evidence.outcome: Model performance across racial subgroups (Asian, Black, White) for glaucoma detection
evidence.effect: CNN Overall AUC 0.80, LSTM 0.01 lower. Both models showed disparities and biases across racial groups; CNN showed reduced group disparities compared to LSTM.
evidence.quote: Both models showed disparities and biases in performance across different racial groups.

evidence.title: Prospective multicenter external validation of the rib fracture frailty index
evidence.venue: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
evidence.outcome: RFF Index performance across lower versus higher Injury Severity Score subgroups
evidence.effect: Higher predictive performance over age was limited to patients with lower injury burden (ISS <15); both models had poor calibration for discharge home after hospitalization >=5 days.
evidence.quote: The RFF score had higher discrimination (OR, 0.09; 95% CI, 0.08-0.11 vs. OR, 0.06; 95% CI, 0.04-0.08; p = 0.04) and calibration performance compared with age, but on secondary analysis, higher predictive performance was limited to patients with lower injury burden.

evidence.title: Comparison of different Lunit INSIGHT CXR software versions when reading chest radiographs for tuberculosis
evidence.outcome: AUC differences across demographic and clinical subgroups
evidence.effect: Newer software improved AUC in past TB 0.67 vs 0.73 (p=0.003), older individuals 0.75 vs 0.77 (p=0.040), and males 0.73 vs 0.76 (p=0.008).
evidence.quote: Similarly, there were no significant differences AUCs between the CAD software versions in younger individuals (0.78 vs 0.80, p = 0.425) and females (0.80 vs 0.79, p = 0.875), but the newer v3.9.0.1 software’s AUCs were significantly higher among older individuals (0.75 vs 0.77, p = 0.040) and males (0.73 vs 0.76, p = 0.008).

evidence.title: External Validation of SCORE2-Diabetes Risk Prediction Model in Chinese Patients with Diabetes
evidence.outcome: sex-specific calibration
evidence.effect: Original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women.
evidence.quote: The original SCORE2-Diabetes underestimated risk by 30% in men and 50% in women, whereas the recalibrated SCORE2-Diabetes using high-risk region scaling factor had the best calibration, overestimating risk by only 4% in men and underestimating by 7% in women.

evidence.title: Performance of the Large Language Models in African rheumatology: a diagnostic test accuracy study of ChatGPT-4, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy differences across age subgroups and disease categories
evidence.effect: Patients under 50 had significantly higher odds of correct diagnosis with Copilot (OR = 3.36; 95% CI 1.16-9.71; p = 0.025); ChatGPT-4 and Claude sensitivity <67% for neoplastic diseases.
evidence.quote: Patients under 50 years old had a significantly higher probability of receiving a correct diagnosis with Copilot (OR = 3.36; 95% CI [1.16-9.71]; p = 0.025).

evidence.title: Development of the treatment prediction model in the artificial intelligence in depression - medication enhancement study
evidence.outcome: Model bias amplification across demographic subgroups
evidence.effect: The model was examined for biases and did not amplify potentially harmful biases; AUC on held-out test set was 0.65.
evidence.quote: The model did not amplify potentially harmful biases.
evidence.sample_unit: adults with moderate to severe major depression from antidepressant clinical trials

evidence.title: A deep learning system for detecting systemic lupus erythematosus from retinal images
evidence.outcome: DeepSLE performance across gender, age, ethnicity, and socioeconomic subgroups
evidence.effect: Robust performance reported across subgroups stratified by gender, age, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status; overall AUCs of 0.822-0.969 for SLE in multi-ethnic validation datasets.
evidence.quote: Additionally, DeepSLE demonstrates robust performance across subgroups stratified by gender, age, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status.

evidence.title: Digital Phenotyping for Detecting Depression Severity in a Large Payor-Provider System: Retrospective Study of Speech and Language Model Performance
evidence.outcome: Model concordance with PHQ-8 across age, sex, and Social Vulnerability Index subgroups
evidence.effect: Performance maintained across subgroups, with concordance correlation coefficients ρc=0.44-0.61; overall ρc=0.54 on the Blind Set.
evidence.quote: This performance was maintained when dividing each set into subgroups of age brackets (≤39, 40-64, and ≥65 years), biological sex, and the 4 categories of Social Vulnerability Index (an index based on 16 social factors), with concordance correlation coefficients ranging as ρc=0.44-0.61.

evidence.title: Comparing ChatGPT3.5 and Bard recommendations for colonoscopy intervals: Bridging the gap in healthcare settings
evidence.outcome: LLM concordance with panel by hospital setting (safety-net vs private)
evidence.effect: Safety-net: GPT3.5 60.5% vs Bard 45.7% (P<0.001); private: 60.3% vs 54.3% (P=0.13). Bard kappa 0.148 safety-net vs 0.282 private.
evidence.quote: In the safety-net hospital, GPT3.5 had a 60.5% concordance rate with the panel compared with Bard's 45.7% ( P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Clinical Context Is More Important than Data Quantity to the Performance of an Artificial Intelligence-Based Early Warning System
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination across high versus moderate/low Charlson Comorbidity Index subgroups
evidence.effect: Discriminative ability remained robust across both CCI groups despite differing volumes of laboratory data and missing values.
evidence.quote: The discriminative ability of the model remained robust across both groups, implying that the clinical context of missingness outweighed the raw quantity of available data.

evidence.title: Deep learning for pediatric chest x-ray diagnosis: Repurposing a commercial tool developed for adults
evidence.outcome: Subgroup performance by age group, masked by aggregate metrics
evidence.effect: AUC 0.91 (accuracy 78%) in ages 2-6 vs AUC 0.96 (accuracy 89.7%) in ages 7-14, p<0.001.
evidence.quote: In the younger age group (n = 509 [53.1%]; mean age 3.7 ± 1.4 years), the AUC for the presence of any relevant finding was 0.91 (95% CI: 0.88–0.94), with an accuracy of 78% (95% CI: 74.1–81.5%) and a sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of 88.1%, 74%, 57% and 94.1%, respectively.

evidence.title: Algorithmic Fairness in Machine Learning Prediction of Autism Using Electronic Health Records
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Model performance and fairness metrics (equal opportunity, equalized odds) by sex for ASD prediction
evidence.effect: Significant fairness issues were found in ML models for ASD prediction using EHRs when performance was compared between boys and girls (equal opportunity and equalized odds).
evidence.quote: Our results revealed significant fairness issues in ML models for ASD prediction using EHRs.
evidence.sample_unit: children (70,803 with ASD and 212,409 matched controls)

evidence.title: Performance of Open-Source Large Language Models in Psychiatry: Usability Study Through Comparative Analysis of Non-English Records and English Translations
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy by input language (Korean vs English)
evidence.effect: Top-1 accuracy 59% (Korean) vs 74.5% (English), P<.001; top-2 accuracy comparable (90% vs 89.5%, P=.56).
evidence.quote: For all 200 notes, the Korean input achieved a top-1 accuracy of 59% (n=118), while the English-translated input performed better, with a top-1 accuracy of 74.5% (n=149).

evidence.title: Moving beyond word error rate to evaluate automatic speech recognition in clinical samples: Lessons from research into schizophrenia-spectrum disorders
evidence.outcome: ASR word error rate variation across patient subgroups (country of birth, positive symptom severity)
evidence.effect: WER ranged from 0.31 to 0.58 across 50 samples, with systematic variations by country of birth and severity of positive symptoms.
evidence.quote: Different WER showed systematic variations based on country of birth and severity of positive symptoms.

evidence.title: Deep Learning with Disc Photos or OCT Scans in Glaucoma Detection
evidence.outcome: AUC of glaucoma detection models across race, sex, and ethnicity subgroups
evidence.effect: OCT model AUCs 0.93, 0.92, 0.92 for Asians, Blacks, Whites (P<0.005); 0.89 women vs 0.93 men (P=0.005); DP model race AUCs 0.87, 0.90, 0.82 (P<0.005).
evidence.quote: The OCT and DP model accuracies varied significantly by demographic groups.
evidence.sample_unit: OCT and disc photo image sets

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence for Management of Major Depression: Initial Design, Progress, and Research Plans
evidence.outcome: Subgroup accuracy of antidepressant response predictions, African American patients vs. others
evidence.effect: Adjustments were needed to improve accuracy for African Americans for 4 antidepressants; none were needed for the remaining 10 antidepressants.
evidence.quote: In component 2, the use of the system required adjustments to improve accuracy for predicting the responses of African Americans to four antidepressants and no adjustments were required for the remaining 10 antidepressants.
evidence.sample_unit: Virginia residents using the advice system

evidence.title: Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence vs Professionally Translated Discharge Instructions
evidence.outcome: AI translation fluency, adequacy, meaning and error severity by language versus professional translation
evidence.effect: Pooled AI fluency 2.98 vs 3.90 for professional translations (difference 0.92; P<.001). Spanish was noninferior in adequacy and error severity, but Chinese, Vietnamese and Somali were inferior on all metrics, worst for Somali.
evidence.quote: The Chinese, Vietnamese, and Somali AI translations were inferior to the professional translations across all metrics, with the greatest differences for Somali.

evidence.title: Evaluating the impact of data biases on algorithmic fairness and clinical utility of machine learning models for prolonged opioid use prediction
evidence.outcome: Subgroup gaps masked by aggregate metrics
evidence.effect: Forest plots revealed subgroup-level disparities masked by overall cohort metrics; opioid-exposed subgroup had greatest performance and net benefit degradation.
evidence.quote: Forest plots revealed subgroup-level disparities in performance that were masked by overall cohort metrics.

evidence.title: The Potential of AI in Nursing Care: Multicenter Evaluation in Fall Risk Assessment
evidence.outcome: Model fairness across sex and age subgroups
evidence.effect: No performance disparities between sex groups, but fairness infringements found across age groups.
evidence.quote: Our fairness analysis ruled out disparities in model performance between different sex groups, but we found fairness infringements across age groups.

evidence.title: Evaluating human-in-the-loop strategies for artificial intelligence-enabled translation of patient discharge instructions: a multidisciplinary analysis
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT-4o translation quality ratings across six languages relative to professional translation
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o rated poorest for Armenian and Somali (Armenian overall quality 2.4 vs professional 3.6, p<0.001); lower for Chinese and Arabic; comparable for Bengali and Spanish.
evidence.quote: Relative to professional translations, evaluators rated all domains for ChatGPT-4o most poorly for Armenian and Somali.
evidence.sample_unit: evaluators (12 linguists, 16 clinicians, 14 family caregivers) rating 20 discharge instruction texts translated into 6 languages

evidence.title: Assessment of demographic bias in retinal age prediction machine learning models
evidence.outcome: Retinal age prediction error (MAE) and age gap differences by sex and ethnicity across imaging modalities
evidence.effect: Combined CFP+OCT MAE 3.01 years vs CFP 3.40 and OCT 4.37. Significant sex differences only in CFP model (p<0.001); significant ethnicity differences only in OCT model (p<0.001); none in combined model.
evidence.quote: Significant sex differences were observed only in the CFP model (p < 0.001), while significant ethnicity differences appeared only in the OCT model (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: AI-Powered Chest X-Ray for Diagnosing Pulmonary Tuberculosis in County and Township Health Care Facilities in Yichang: Retrospective, Real-World Study
evidence.outcome: CAD PPV by age subgroup
evidence.effect: Age ≥80 had lower PPV: OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.10‐0.44; P <.001.
evidence.quote: Multivariate logistic regression also demonstrated that advanced age (≥80 y) groups were less likely to achieve high PPV (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.10‐0.44; P <.001).

evidence.title: Performance of a deep learning-based algorithm for automated measurements of Cobb angles on preoperative spine radiographs in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
evidence.outcome: AI measurement error by scoliosis severity subgroup (moderate, severe, extreme)
evidence.effect: For extreme scoliosis, AI MAE was 6.53° (95%CI 5.06–7.86) versus residents' 3.61° (95%CI 3.17–3.97), P<0.001; no significant difference between moderate and severe (P=0.86).
evidence.quote: For extreme scoliosis, the MAE of the AI (6.53° [95%CI 5.06°, 7.86°]) was significantly higher than that of the residents (3.61° [95%CI, 3.17°, 3.97°]) (P<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: Cobb angles on preoperative whole spine radiographs

evidence.title: Comparative validation of PREDICT versions 3.1 and 2.2 for overall survival in the Dutch breast cancer population
evidence.outcome: Performance across 36 subgroups by ER, HER2, age and tumour stage
evidence.effect: v3.1 generally outperformed v2.2 except age >75, where v2.2 was more accurate; in ER-/HER2- aged 50-75, v3.1 overestimated 1.5-2.8% and v2.2 underestimated 2.8-5.3%.
evidence.quote: Across subgroups, v3.1 generally outperformed v2.2 except in patients aged >75 years, where v2.2 provided more accurate estimates.

evidence.title: Connecting algorithmic fairness and fair outcomes in a sociotechnical simulation case study of AI-assisted healthcare
evidence.outcome: Impact of subgroup TPR/FPR disparities in AI on group-wise outcomes
evidence.effect: Lowering unprivileged TPR by 30% increased mortality rate ratio by over 15%; 30% higher privileged FPR reduced ratio by under 5%.
evidence.quote: For instance, at a given ΔFPR, lowering the TPR for the unprivileged group by 30% increased the mortality rate ratio by over 15%.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated women per run (100 simulation runs)

evidence.title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination and calibration by racial/ethnic subgroup
evidence.effect: C-index ranged 0.78 to 0.89 across groups; calibration poorest for Black patients, with risk underestimation.
evidence.quote: Calibration is poorest for Black patients, but SMI was the best among all three imputation strategies ( Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: Evaluation and improvement of algorithmic fairness for COVID-19 severity classification using Explainable Artificial Intelligence-based bias mitigation
evidence.outcome: Sex-based accuracy parity difference of baseline COVID-19 severity model
evidence.effect: Baseline model achieved 90.68% accuracy but exhibited a 10.11% Subset Accuracy Parity Difference between sexes, indicating a relatively large bias.
evidence.quote: The baseline (unmitigated) classification model achieved 90.68% accuracy but exhibited a 10.11% Subset Accuracy Parity Difference between sexes, indicating a relatively large bias.

evidence.title: Assessing the safety of patient-centred discharge medication instructions generated by an AI model
evidence.outcome: Proportion of cases with at least one potential safety issue, compared across age, complexity, insurance
evidence.effect: Safety issues differed across age groups (p = 0.031), patient complexity (p < 0.001) and insurance types (p = 0.047); medication correctness and UMS format did not differ by group.
evidence.quote: There was evidence of a difference in the proportion of cases with at least one potential safety issue across age groups (p = 0.031), patient complexity (p < 0.001) and insurance types (p = 0.047).

evidence.title: A Novel Multimodal Implementation of a Foundation Artificial Intelligence Model Using Optic Nerve Head Fundus Photographs and OCT Imaging for Glaucoma Detection
evidence.outcome: Glaucoma detection AUC stratified by race, age, and disease severity
evidence.effect: No significant differences by race or age in unimodal or multimodal models. All models performed better for moderate-to-severe than mild glaucoma, significant for CFP (P=0.002) and OCT (P=0.005) unimodal models.
evidence.quote: No significant differences based on race or age were found in either unimodal or multimodal glaucoma detection models.

evidence.title: Learning neuroimaging models from health system-scale data
evidence.outcome: Algorithmic fairness of diagnostic performance across sensitive patient groups
evidence.effect: Abstract reports Prima demonstrates algorithmic fairness across sensitive groups; no subgroup metrics given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Prima demonstrates algorithmic fairness across sensitive groups.

evidence.title: Mechanistic interpretability of reinforcement learning in Medicaid care coordination
evidence.outcome: Residual harm rates among cleared decisions by race/ethnicity and sex subgroup
evidence.effect: Baseline residual harm varied from 1.03% (Hispanic) to 1.33% (non-Hispanic black, p=0.006); female 1.14% vs male 1.28%.
evidence.quote: Baseline residual harm varied from 1.03% (Hispanic) to 1.33% (non-Hispanic black, p=0.006).

evidence.title: Accuracy of the GPT-5 Mini in Predicting Six-Week Postoperative Knee Flexion Following Total Knee Replacement: A Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: GPT-5 mini prediction error in knee flexion across patient subgroups (age, ASA grade, diabetes, smoking, BMI)
evidence.effect: Median actual flexion 95° vs predicted 103°; median absolute error 10°. Absolute error differed by ASA grade (I: 17°, II: 9°, III: 6°, p < 0.001). BMI showed no association with error.
evidence.quote: Absolute error differed significantly by ASA grade (I: 17°, II: 9°, III: 6°, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Predicting Anticipated Telehealth Use: Development of the CONTEST Score and Machine Learning Models Using a National U.S. Survey
evidence.outcome: Group fairness metrics (Disparate Impact, Equal Opportunity) across sex and race/ethnicity
evidence.effect: Group fairness metrics revealed disparities across sex and race/ethnicity; individual counterfactual flip rates were low (sex CFR 0.024; race/ethnicity CFR 0.013).
evidence.quote: Group fairness metrics revealed disparities across sex and race/ethnicity, whereas individual counterfactual analyses indicated low flip rates (sex CFR: 0.024; race/ethnicity CFR: 0.013).
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents with at least one telehealth visit in prior 12 months (HINTS 7)

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of large language models as decision support tools in oral pathology
evidence.outcome: LLM performance variation by patient age and sex subgroups
evidence.effect: Increasing patient age was associated with mild but significant reduction in performance for ChatGPT-4.0, Meta AI, and Gemini; no age effect for ChatGPT o1-preview; sex had no significant impact.
evidence.quote: Increasing patient age was associated with a mild but statistically significant reduction in model performance for ChatGPT-4.0, Meta AI, and Gemini, while no significant age effect was observed for ChatGPT o1-preview; patient sex had no significant impact.

evidence.title: Fairness analysis of machine learning predictions of aggression in acute psychiatric care
evidence.outcome: Disparities in false positive and true positive rates of aggression prediction across demographic and social subgroups
evidence.effect: Random forest ROC-AUC 0.81 overall; significant FPR and TPR disparities across subgroups, with higher FPR for Middle Eastern and Black patients, men, police-admitted patients, and those with unstable or supportive housing.
evidence.quote: Fairness analyses revealed significant disparities in FPR and TPR across subgroups: FPR was higher for Middle Eastern and Black patients, men, those admitted into emergency care by the police, and those with unstable or supportive forms of housing.

evidence.title: Accent related errors in clinical speech transcription and a LLM-based remedy
evidence.outcome: subgroup transcription performance gap
evidence.effect: Non-native speakers consistently had higher WER; effect sizes varied by model, with Whisper β = 11.0 and WhisperX β = 3.4.
evidence.quote: Across all three ASR systems (Whisper, WhisperX, and WhisperX-GPT) non-native speakers consistently demonstrated higher WER, with the effect size varying by model.

evidence.title: Predictive divergence in machine learning models for clinical mortality risk: A multicohort study of covid-19 patients
evidence.outcome: Model performance variation across k-means patient subgroups versus aggregate performance
evidence.effect: Overall performance was high (µ = 0.855), but performance varied significantly within five clinical clusters (F = 73.18, p < 0.001); TabPFN underperformed in the Immunodeficient cluster.
evidence.quote: Unsupervised k-means clustering identified five clinically distinct patient subgroups with mortality rates ranging from 22% to 80%, within which model performance varied significantly (F = 73.18, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Diagnostic accuracy, fairness and clinical implementation of AI for breast cancer screening: results of multicenter retrospective and prospective technical feasibility studies
evidence.outcome: Demographic subgroup performance disparities of the AI system
evidence.effect: No systematic demographic disparities were observed in the retrospective analysis.
evidence.quote: No systematic demographic disparities were observed.

evidence.title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Data Replicates Clinical Prediction Performance in a Million-Patient Diabetes Cohort
evidence.outcome: Sex-stratified bias in synthetic data versus real data not visible in standard metrics
evidence.effect: Bias and domain-specific sex-stratified analyses reveal inconsistencies not discernible through standard metrics, despite comparable aggregate predictive performance.
evidence.quote: However, bias and domain-specific sex-stratified analyses reveal inconsistencies not discernible through standard metrics, while data augmentation provides no performance benefit, as data saturation is reached given the large source population.

evidence.title: An artificial intelligence prediction model for optimizing patient selection for cardiac imaging for the investigation of suspected coronary artery disease
evidence.outcome: ethnicity subgroup AUROC
evidence.effect: Local model AUROC was 0.704 [95% CI: 0.702, 0.705] for Asian patients and 0.612 [95% CI: 0.609, 0.614] for Black patients.
evidence.quote: The local model performed best for Asian patients (AUROC = 0.704 [95% CI: 0.702, 0.705]) and worst for Black patients (AUROC = 0.612 [95% CI: 0.609, 0.614]).
evidence.sample_unit: elective outpatients undergoing invasive coronary angiography

evidence.title: DeepSeek-R1 performance in fusion planning of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: A preliminary study
evidence.outcome: Rate of surgically reasonable fusion levels by Lenke curve subtype
evidence.effect: Overall 70.9% (144/203) reasonable; varied significantly by Lenke subtype: high for 1A (87.0%), 1B (82.9%), 5C (81.1%), 6C (87.5%), low for 1C (19.0%), 2A (42.9%), 2C (25.0%).
evidence.quote: Performance varied significantly by Lenke subtype, demonstrating high reasonable rates for types 1A (87.0%), 1B (82.9%), 5C (81.1%), and 6C (87.5%).

evidence.title: Improving Fairness and Mitigating Bias in Multicenter Electronic Health Records Models to Predict Glaucoma Outcomes
evidence.outcome: Subgroup fairness gaps (equalized odds by sex and race/ethnicity) across internal and external sites
evidence.effect: Baseline and column remover had sex EO >0.298; a trade-off was seen between AUROC and equalized odds gaps across sites, with no method excelling on both.
evidence.quote: For sex EO, baseline and column remover performed poorly (EO > 0.298 [0.276, 0.322]), while adversarial classifier (EO < 0.220 [0.191, 0.257]) and, to some extent, threshold optimization performed better across test sets (EO < 0.243 [0.213, 0.299]).

evidence.title: A prospective multicenter trial of deep learning auto-segmentation for organs at risk in thoracic radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: AI segmentation accuracy differences between lung cancer and non-lung-cancer patients
evidence.effect: AI accuracy was significantly lower for the heart, trachea, and esophagus in lung cancer patients; no consistent multi-metric differences occurred for lungs or bronchial tree. Numerical effect sizes were not reported.
evidence.quote: In patients with LC, the model’s segmentation accuracy (i.e., AI-vDSC, HD95, and sDSC) for the heart, trachea, and esophagus was significantly lower than in non-LC patients; however, no consistent multi-metric differences were observed for the lungs and bronchial tree (Supplementary Fig. 8 ).

evidence.title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
evidence.outcome: Age- and education-related differences in comprehension of AI-simplified reports
evidence.effect: Older participants had better comprehension within both educational strata: Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.32 for high education and 0.41 for low education; adjusted P < 0.05.
evidence.quote: Results indicated significant differences: younger and older participants differed notably in understanding the reports, with older participants showing better comprehension than younger, both in high-education groups (Group 1 vs. Group 3；effect size Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.32; 95% CI: 0.21, 0.39) and low-education groups (Group 2 vs. Group 4；effect size Cliff’s |Δ| = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.32, 0.53) (adjusted P < 0.05 after Bonferroni correction; Fig. 2c, d ).
evidence.sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

evidence.title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
evidence.venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination across racial/ethnic, Medicaid, and rural subgroups
evidence.effect: AUC was lower in Black (0.63-0.65), Medicaid (0.64-0.67), and rural (0.65-0.66) groups than overall (0.68-0.69) with the original model.
evidence.quote: AUC decreased when models were run separately among Black, Hispanic, Medicaid-insured, and rural residents.

evidence.title: Multicenter validation and updating of the ELDER-ICU model for severity assessment in elderly critical illness
evidence.outcome: Subgroup discrimination heterogeneity
evidence.effect: Sex differences were pronounced in Asian sites; AUROCs were consistently higher among females.
evidence.quote: Sex-based differences were negligible in the US and Austrian cohorts but pronounced in the Asian sites, where AUROCs were consistently higher among females than males.

commentary.bottom_line: Across 30 studies, subgroup and site analyses repeatedly found performance gaps that aggregate metrics concealed, including a 9% higher false-negative rate in female adolescents and site-level AUROCs ranging from 0.608 to 0.851. No study tested whether evaluating subgroups before deployment changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: Of 30 studies, two were prospective in real deployment (108 visits and 8,493 patients), and most were offline retrospective analyses. They consistently show that subgroup analysis is feasible and often finds gaps that aggregate metrics hide. No study compared deployments with and without such evaluation, so certainty that the practice improves outcomes is low.

In pediatric anxiety prediction, female adolescents had 4% lower accuracy and 9% higher false-negative rates than males, and aggregate results did not show this gap. A deployed suicide risk model had a 77% false-negative rate in transgender patients. These findings suggest subgroup review may catch missed-diagnosis risks early, though no study showed that it prevented harm.

Performance varied by site in several studies. Local AUROC ranged from 0.608 to 0.851 across sites for coronary angiography decisions, error rates differed by cancer registry and by geography, and fairness metrics passed in one dataset and failed in another. This pattern suggests vendor or single-site results may not transfer to a new setting.

Three tests included safety-net or Medicaid patients, and none included limited English proficiency or low-literacy groups. In a Brazilian cohort, AUC was 0.57 for mixed-race participants versus 0.77 overall. An intersectional analysis found a sex-by-age gap 5.2 times the single-attribute gap, which suggests single-attribute checks may miss disparities.

FDA draft guidance asks developers to report subgroup analysis by sex, age, race, ethnicity, disease severity, site, and equipment. A review found subgroup analyses reported for 11 of 26 authorized devices with change-control plans, and none of these analyses included patient outcomes. This finding suggests health systems may not be able to rely on submission data for subgroup assurance.

Subgroup testing requires enough cases per group. A GPT-4 evaluation on 539 notes found error-rate differences with overlapping confidence intervals, and some groups had fewer than five patients. One triage study set a prespecified F1 gap threshold of 0.05 and found a 0.020 gender gap, which shows one way to make subgroup review a pass-fail step.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared AI deployments that underwent pre-deployment subgroup and site evaluation with deployments that did not, measuring either the deployment decisions made or patient outcomes. Methods for evaluating small subgroups and intersectional groups with adequate precision remain untested in real deployment. Language and literacy subgroups have not been examined in tests of the practice.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests included Medicaid, low-income, or safety-net patients. One was a real-deployment study of 225 patients, 69.0% of whom were African American, and two were offline analyses. No test included limited English proficiency or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore says nothing about how subgroup evaluation performs for language and literacy groups, and systems serving those patients would need to define and test those subgroups locally.
